keyword: what do bed bugs look like
metaTitle: What Do Bed Bugs Look Like? Size, Color, Stages
metaDescription: Adult bed bugs are flat, oval, reddish-brown and 3/16 to 1/4 inch long, like an apple seed. Sizes for eggs and all five nymph stages, plus mattress signs.
h1: What Do Bed Bugs Look Like? Size, Shape and Color at Every Life Stage
dek: An identification guide to the bug itself: adult size in inches, how a blood meal changes its shape and color, the five nymph stages, the eggs, and what you actually see on a mattress or on skin.
excerpt: Adult bed bugs are flat, oval, reddish-brown and 3/16 to 1/4 inch long. See how big each nymph stage is, what the eggs look like, and how a fed bug changes color.

quickAnswer.lead: **An adult bed bug is a flat, oval, brown to reddish-brown insect with no working wings, about 3/16 to 1/4 inch long (5 to 7 mm), close to the size of an apple seed**, according to [the EPA's description of bed bug appearance](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/bed-bugs-appearance-and-life-cycle). After a blood meal it swells, lengthens and turns red. Nymphs are smaller and nearly see-through, and eggs are pearl-white specks the size of a pinhead.
bullets: Adults measure 3/16 to 1/4 inch (5 to 7 mm), and the University of Tennessee notes a large female can reach 1/3 inch.
An unfed adult is flat and brown; within a couple of hours of feeding it is swollen, elongated and bright red.
There are five nymph stages, growing from about 1/16 inch (1.5 mm) to just under 3/16 inch (4.5 mm).
Eggs are about 0.04 inch (1 mm) long, pearl-white, and show an eye spot once they are more than five days old.
On a mattress, check the seams for black fecal dots, pale shed skins and eggs rather than expecting bugs in the open.
A feeding can take 3 to 12 minutes, after which the bug crawls away to hide, so you are unlikely to find one on skin.

body.text: What does an adult bed bug look like?

An adult bed bug is a flat, oval, reddish-brown insect with no working wings, about 3/16 to 1/4 inch long (5 to 7 mm). [The EPA's page on bed bug appearance](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/bed-bugs-appearance-and-life-cycle) sizes it against an apple seed. An adult that has not fed recently is so flat that Virginia Tech entomologist Dini Miller compares it to a disc in [her guide to identifying a bed bug infestation](https://www.vdacs.virginia.gov/pdf/bb-identify1.pdf).

Look closer and the EPA's list of true-bug features applies: a beak with three segments, antennae with four parts, wings that are not used for flying, and short, golden-colored hairs. Bed bugs do not fly, and they do not jump the way fleas do, but the [University of Kentucky's bed bug fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef636) notes that they crawl rapidly across floors, walls and ceilings.

Males and females differ at the rear end. [The University of Tennessee's bed bug identification page](https://bedbugs.tennessee.edu/biology-and-identification/) describes the abdominal tip of the common bed bug, *Cimex lectularius*, as pointed in males and rounded in females, and says an adult female can be up to 1/3 inch long and nearly 1/4 inch wide. That is above the EPA's range, so a fair reading of the two sources together is 3/16 to 1/4 inch as the typical adult size and 1/3 inch as Tennessee's upper figure for a female.
Identification is the first step, not the whole job. The [complete bed bug reference](/learn/bed-bugs) picks up where this page stops, with biology, how infestations start and every treatment option.

body.text: How big is a bed bug next to everyday objects?

items: **An apple seed.** The standard comparison for an adult, used by both the EPA and Virginia Tech.
**A lentil.** The University of Kentucky says an adult matches an apple seed in color but is closer to a lentil in size.

**Lincoln's head on a penny.** [The CDC's bed bug overview](https://www.cdc.gov/bed-bugs/about/index.html) uses this for the insect's full size range of 1 mm to 7 mm, which is roughly 0.04 to 1/4 inch.

**The edge of a credit card.** [The EPA's guide to finding bed bugs](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) uses a credit card to show how thin a bed bug is, which is why it can squeeze into very small hiding spots.
**A pinhead.** The EPA's comparison for an egg, and the University of Kentucky's for a newly hatched nymph.

body.text: What color are bed bugs before and after feeding?

A bed bug that has not fed recently is brown to reddish-brown, and one that has just fed is red and swollen. The EPA describes the unfed adult as long, brown, flat and oval, and the recently fed adult as balloon-like, reddish-brown and more elongated. Virginia Tech's guide adds the timing: within a couple of hours of a blood meal the body is bright red and shaped more like a torpedo than a disc, and over the next couple of days it darkens and flattens again as the blood is digested.

Nymphs change with a blood meal too. A hungry nymph is almost completely pale white or yellowish. Once it feeds it plumps up and turns brilliant red, and Virginia Tech compares it at that point to a plump raspberry seed. A nymph is easiest to spot right after it has eaten.

body.caption: Descriptions from the EPA and from Virginia Tech's bed bug identification guide.

body.text: Because color tracks digestion, two bed bugs from the same bed can look like different insects. If the one you found is very dark, the guide to [whether bed bugs are ever black](/blog/black-bed-bugs) goes through the darker shades and the small black insects that get mistaken for them.
What do baby bed bugs (nymphs) look like at each of the five stages?

Baby bed bugs, called nymphs, look like miniature adults with translucent or whitish-yellow bodies, and they grow from about 1/16 inch (1.5 mm) at hatching to just under 3/16 inch (4.5 mm) before the final molt. There are five nymph stages, also called instars. The EPA publishes a length for each stage in millimeters; the inch figures below are converted from those.

The same pale, see-through body, visible to the naked eye

body.text: Every stage has to take a blood meal before it can molt to the next, so a nymph sheds its skin five times on the way to adulthood. Under favorable conditions, which the University of Kentucky gives as 70 to 80°F with a ready supply of blood, a bed bug can mature in as little as a month. Cooler temperatures or limited access to a host stretch that out.

One limit worth knowing: the sources describe nymph color as a group, not stage by stage. Apart from length, none of the agency or extension pages read for this guide gives a marking that separates a third-stage nymph from a fourth. If you need to judge a very young bug, the page on [what baby bed bugs look like and what finding one means](/blog/baby-bed-bugs-nymphs) stays with the early stages.

body.text: What do bed bug eggs look like?

Bed bug eggs are pearl-white, elongated and about 0.04 inch (1 mm) long, roughly the size of a pinhead. The EPA says an egg more than five days old carries a visible eye spot. The University of Kentucky compares an egg to a speck of dust and says the eggs are hard to see without magnification, especially on light-colored materials.

Eggs do not roll loose. The University of Kentucky says they are sticky when first laid, which makes them adhere to surfaces, and the University of Tennessee describes the female cementing each one in place. Females lay them in secluded places at a rate the EPA puts at 1 to 3 eggs per day. At room temperature they hatch in about a week according to the University of Kentucky; the University of Tennessee gives six to 10 days. Hatched and unhatched eggs turn up together in the places where the bugs hide.

body.title: Use magnification
body.text: Eggs and first-stage nymphs sit at the limit of what the unaided eye can pick out. Check seams with a magnifying glass and strong light before deciding a mattress is clear.
What do bed bugs look like on a mattress?

On a mattress, bed bugs show up as flat brown bugs tucked into the seams together with what they leave behind: black dots, pale shed skins, tiny white eggs and rusty smears. The bugs hide when they are not feeding, so look for the evidence as well as the insects. The EPA lists all of these among the physical signs of bed bugs, and Virginia Tech's guide explains how to recognize the fecal spots, the shed skins and the clusters of bugs.

items: **Black fecal spots.** Digested blood dries black, not red, and the spots often appear in groups of 10 or more. The EPA sizes each one at about a printed bullet point and says it can bleed into fabric the way a marker would.

**A smooth feel.** Virginia Tech notes that bed bug spots feel smooth because they are a dried liquid, while German cockroach droppings feel granular. The University of Tennessee adds that bed bug feces run red when moistened and cockroach feces do not.
**Shed skins.** Each one is the same shape as a bed bug but translucent and hollow, like an empty shell, in sizes that match the five nymph stages. The EPA describes them as pale yellow.
**Eggs and eggshells.** Pearl-white, about 0.04 inch (1 mm) long, and stuck to the surface.
**Rusty or reddish stains.** The EPA attributes these to bed bugs that were crushed on the sheets or mattress.
**Live bugs.** Virginia Tech notes that bed bugs gather in groups after feeding, so live bugs often turn up clustered, with several life stages in the same spot.

body.text: Virginia Tech's list of places to look for these clusters starts at the bed: along the mattress seams, in the tufts, under the mattress tags, where the box spring fabric is stapled to its wood frame, and behind the headboard. The CDC says bed bugs tend to live within 8 feet of where people sleep, so the search widens from the bed outward; the guide to [where bed bugs hide beyond the mattress](/blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide) ranks those spots by distance.

If your seams match this description, [what to do about bed bugs on a mattress](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress) covers cleaning, encasing and whether the mattress has to go. If you are not sure the dots came from bed bugs at all, compare them against [bed bug fecal stains and the marks most often confused with them](/blog/bed-bug-stains-poop-droppings-canada).

body.text: What do bed bugs look like on skin?

You are unlikely to see a bed bug on skin, because it feeds for only a few minutes and then leaves. The University of Kentucky puts a feeding at about three to 10 minutes and the EPA at 3 to 12 minutes. The University of Kentucky adds that bed bugs normally do not reside on or attach to people the way lice or ticks do; immediately after feeding they crawl to a secluded place to digest the meal. If you do catch one in the act, it will be filling out and turning red as described above.

That behavior is a useful clue in itself. A small brown bug that is fastened to the skin and will not brush away is acting like a tick, and the comparison of [ticks and bed bugs side by side](/blog/tick-vs-bed-bug) shows how the two differ.

What stays on the skin is the bite. The CDC describes bed bug bites as similar to mosquito or flea bites: a slightly swollen, red area that may itch, either scattered at random or in a straight line. The University of Kentucky says the bugs bite skin left exposed during sleep, such as the face, neck, shoulders, back, arms and legs. Timing varies widely. The CDC says marks can take as long as 14 days to develop in some people, and the University of Kentucky cites studies in infested apartments suggesting that about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly.

The EPA calls bites on the skin a poor indicator of an infestation: they can look like bites from other insects, like rashes or like hives, and some people do not react to bed bug bites at all. Skin can raise the suspicion; only the bug or its signs can confirm it. The page on [what bed bug bites look like and how long they last](/blog/bed-bug-bites) covers the skin side in full.

body.title: When to call a healthcare provider
body.text: The CDC says bed bugs are not known to spread diseases to people, but it lists enlarged bite marks, painful swelling at the bite site and, on rare occasions, anaphylaxis as possible allergic symptoms. If you think you are having an allergic reaction to bed bug bites, speak with your healthcare provider.
How do you confirm that the bug you found is a bed bug?

Confirm it by checking the specimen against the features on this page and, if any doubt is left, having an entomologist examine it. The EPA calls accurate identification a critical first step, because many bugs look like bed bugs and treating for the wrong one is costly. The University of Kentucky notes that bed bugs are sometimes mistaken for ticks, cockroaches, carpet beetles and other household insects, and that close relatives that feed on bats or birds can be told apart from bed bugs by an entomologist or pest professional.

items: **Measure it.** An adult is 3/16 to 1/4 inch long (5 to 7 mm), and a nymph is smaller. The University of Tennessee's upper figure for a female is 1/3 inch, so a bug well beyond that is unlikely to be a bed bug.
**Check the outline.** Unfed, the body is a broad, flat oval. Fed, it is swollen and more elongated.
**Check the color.** Adults are brown to reddish-brown, hungry nymphs are see-through or whitish-yellow, and any stage is red soon after a meal.
**Watch how it moves.** A bed bug crawls. It does not fly, and it does not hop like a flea.
**Look at what is around it.** Black fecal spots, shed skins and eggs in the same seam or crevice point strongly to bed bugs.

**Keep the specimen.** Seal it in a small container or a zip-top bag so that someone qualified can examine it. The EPA notes that your state cooperative extension service office may be able to help with identification.

body.text: Do not use smell as a test. The EPA describes a musty, sweetish odor produced by glands on the underside of the body, but the University of Kentucky cautions that the smell is seldom apparent except in extreme infestations and should not be relied on for detection.

If your bug fails one of the checks above, work through the [insects most often mistaken for bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs), which compares bat bugs, carpet beetles, spider beetles and others feature by feature. If it passes, move on to the [step-by-step plan for getting rid of bed bugs](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs). And before you reach for a household disinfectant, read [what Lysol does and does not do to bed bugs](/blog/does-lysol-kill-bed-bugs).

faqs.question: Can you see bed bugs with the naked eye?
faqs.answer: Yes for adults, and with some effort for the younger stages. Virginia Tech's identification guide says adults are easily seen without magnification and that all five nymph stages are visible too, only smaller and paler. The first-stage nymph is the hard one: it is tiny and nearly colorless, so it tends to be noticed only when it moves or has just fed and turned red. The EPA says an unfed nymph can be nearly invisible, and the University of Kentucky says eggs are hard to see without magnification.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs have wings, and can they fly or jump?
faqs.answer: Bed bugs cannot fly or jump. The EPA describes them as having wings that are not used for flying, and the University of Tennessee says they lack wings and cannot fly. The University of Kentucky adds that they do not jump like fleas but crawl rapidly over floors, walls and ceilings. The University of Tennessee reports one bed bug timed at about 7.6 feet per minute. A small insect that hops or flies away when disturbed is not a bed bug.

faqs.question: What do bed bug shed skins look like?
faqs.answer: A shed skin looks like a hollow, see-through copy of the bug that left it. Virginia Tech describes molted skins as the same shape as a bed bug, generally translucent, and resembling an empty shell, and the EPA describes them as pale yellow. Because a nymph molts five times before adulthood, the skins come in five sizes. They collect along mattress seams, behind headboards, along baseboards and where walls meet ceilings, and in a larger infestation most are found where the bugs cluster.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs have a smell?
faqs.answer: They can, but smell is not a reliable way to find them. The EPA describes a musty, sweetish odor produced by glands on the underside of the body, and the CDC lists a sweet musty odor among the signs of an infestation. The University of Kentucky cautions that the odor is seldom noticeable except in extreme infestations and should not be relied on for detection. Look for the insects themselves, their black fecal spots, shed skins and eggs instead.

faqs.question: How can you tell a male bed bug from a female?
faqs.answer: The tip of the abdomen is the visible difference. According to the University of Tennessee, an adult male has a pointed abdominal tip and an adult female has a rounded one. The same source says a female can be up to 1/3 inch long and nearly 1/4 inch wide. Telling the sexes apart does not change the next step, because any confirmed bed bug near a bed is a reason to inspect the whole sleeping area for more bugs, eggs and fecal spots.

faqs.question: How long does it take a bed bug to grow from egg to adult?
faqs.answer: As little as a month under favorable conditions. The University of Kentucky says eggs hatch in about a week at room temperature and that bed bugs can mature in as little as a month at 70 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit with a ready supply of blood, molting five times and needing a blood meal before each molt. The EPA gives four to five weeks for the full egg-to-egg cycle under favorable conditions. Cooler temperatures or limited access to a host make development take longer.
